Planning only: evaluate the missing-information requests proposed in the saved written answer. Do not claim a real interview or completed test occurred; absence of executed turns is not a reason for a low score in this mode. Do not require requesting information already in the vignette.

Do not require exact wording or hindsight of hidden diagnosis. Interpret each request against what was known when it could be made.

In his 40s, tinnitus and temporal headache led to diagnosis of a left transverse/sigmoid dural arteriovenous fistula, type IIa+b with venous reflux. Three embolisations relieved symptoms and subsequent MRI remained clear for about 14 years.
In his 50s, pulsatile scalp symptoms, right-sided weakness/numbness and aphasia accompanied a new superior-sagittal-sinus fistula with multiple feeders. Three further embolisations achieved near-occlusion, with about five years of clear follow-up imaging.
In his 60s he developed right occipital pain, retromastoid tenderness and intermittent tinnitus. Angiography in 2018 showed a right transverse/sigmoid fistula classified as type I. The selected record does not specify a new neurological deficit. Later surveillance and symptom outcomes are not supplied. Episode 2 (50s): new superior sagittal sinus fistula with multiple feeders, manifesting as pulsatile scalp symptoms, right‑sided weakness, numbness and aphasia. Three further embolisation procedures produced near‑occlusion; imaging stayed clear for about five years.

Episode 3 (60s): right transverse/sigmoid fistula classified as type I, identified on 2018 angiography after right occipital pain, retromastoid tenderness and intermittent tinnitus. No new neurological deficit is recorded; subsequent surveillance and symptom outcome are not provided.

Key distinctions: the second lesion arose at a different sinus (superior sagittal) and the third at the contralateral transverse/sigmoid junction, indicating new anatomical sites rather than simple recurrence at the original left transverse/sigmoid location.

Features influencing current risk and specialist discussion: (1) multiplicity of distinct dural fistulas over three decades, suggesting a predisposition to de‑novo fistula formation; (2) prior venous reflux (type IIa+b) and high‑grade cortical venous drainage in the first lesion, which carry higher haemorrhagic risk; (3) the recent type I lesion lacks documented cortical venous reflux, but its symptomatic presentation warrants close angiographic surveillance; (4) incomplete long‑term outcome data for the latest lesion limits prognostic certainty.
